Date: 2025-11-18
Start: 15:00 UTC

Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Tom Hayes (CTO, Pacific Orbit), Maya Li (Lead ML Eng), Carlos Ruiz (Infra)

Summary (auto):
Quick technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy for Pacific Orbit's multi-tenant chat assistant. Covered hit-rate expectations, cache key design, tenant isolation, eviction and quotas, interaction with batching and quantization, and implications for on-prem / VPC deployments. Agreed next steps to run synthetic bench, share cache key proposal, and schedule on-prem bench.

Topics:
- Prefix caching hit rates and measurement
- Cache key schema (what to include/hash)
- Multi-tenant safety and namespace isolation
- Interaction with KV cache, batching, and quantization
- VPC/on-prem constraints and security controls
- Eviction policies, cold-starts, and observability

Action items (captured): see metadata above

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Rivera: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're gonna dig into prefix caching and how we would apply it to Pacific Orbit's chat flows. Priya's gonna run through the perf numbers.
[00:18] Priya Singh: hey, hello. um so quick agenda, baseline, hit rates from our internal bench, cache key proposals, and then safety and ops. we'll leave time for your infra questions.
[00:40] Tom Hayes: sounds good. we've got Maya and Carlos on to cover ML and infra, respectively. our main goals are reduce token cost by 30% while keeping tail latency under 300ms p95.
[00:55] Maya Li: yep, and also need to make sure we don't leak tenant prompts between customers, that's non-negotiable.
[01:10] Priya Singh: totally. to start, prefix caching is basically storing the KV cache for the repeated prefix of a prompt so we dont recompute the prefix tokens every request. we see biggest wins on chat where first N tokens repeat across messages.
[01:35] Priya Singh: our internal tests on a hybrid chat workload showed a ~72% hit rate when prefix length is about 8 tokens and template stable. with longer, stable system prompts it went up to mid 80s. but with dynamic prompt assembly (like user-specific context) it drops to around 40-50%.
[01:58] Maya Li: 72% is promising. is that across tenants or single-tenant bench?
[02:07] Priya Singh: that was single-tenant simulated traffic. in multi-tenant we saw effective hit rate fall ~5-15% because of template variance and heterogeneous distribution. eviction noise also reduces effective hits.
[02:25] Carlos Ruiz: what do you mean by eviction noise?
[02:29] Priya Singh: if you share a single global cache pool, noisy tenants with lots of short-lived prefixes will evict stable entries for quieter tenants. so isolation or reservation helps.
[02:45] Alex Rivera: we generally recommend per-tenant namespaces plus soft reservation quotas on Dedicated and Private plans. that buys you isolation without needing fully isolated caches (which is more expensive).
[03:05] Tom Hayes: okay, that makes sense. what's in the cache key? simple tenant + prefix string?
[03:13] Priya Singh: good q. our proposed cache key schema: tenant_id || model_id || prompt_template_hash || prefix_token_length || model_weights_version (or compile id) || quantization_profile. then we hash the whole composite with a keyed HMAC (pepper) so the raw prefix text never sits as plaintext in key stores.
[03:42] Maya Li: so you hash the prompt template not the filled-in user content, right? we want common templates to hit.
[03:50] Priya Singh: exactly — template-level hashing, and we avoid including user PII. for template variants with slot fillers we canonicalize slots before hashing.
[03:59] Carlos Ruiz: how do you handle prompt engineering where teams append customer-specific instructions? that seems like it will fragment the cache.
[04:10] Priya Singh: yep fragmentation is the challenge. we suggest two levers: 1) canonicalization rules to normalize equivalent prefixes; 2) multi-level caching: template-level entries and full-prefix entries. if template-level hits we can warm the KV cache and then apply the small delta for user-specific tokens.
[04:34] Alex Rivera: also note the prefix length; shorter canonical prefixes are more general but hit more often; longer prefixes reduce per-request work more but are less likely to be shared. it's a tradeoff. our bench recommendations show sweet spot around 6-12 tokens for many chat apps.
[04:52] Tom Hayes: you mentioned quantization_profile in keys — how does quantization affect cache reuse?
[04:58] Priya Singh: important point. the KV cache is dependent on internal numerical representation. int8 vs fp16 can yield incompatible KV bytes, so we either normalize by storing cache per quantization profile or store a canonical fp16 cache and transcode when possible. transcoding adds CPU overhead. so we typically include quantization in the key to keep correctness.
[05:22] Maya Li: what's the memory impact if we keep per-profile entries?
[05:26] Priya Singh: it multiplies memory by number of profiles. practically we limit quant profiles per model per deployment; many customers pick one profile in prod to avoid blowup.
[05:36] Carlos Ruiz: for on-prem, our infra might use older GPUs. how does that change caching strategy?
[05:42] Priya Singh: on-prem differences: kernel selection, batch acceleration, and available memory change cache sizing. on H100/A100 we can store larger KV with faster retrieval. on older cards we reduce prefix length or use disk-backed cold cache with async warming.
[06:00] Alex Rivera: for VPC/private deployments, control plane can still orchestrate cache metering, but data plane is in your VPC so we offer per-tenant KMS integration. keys at rest are encrypted via customer's KMS and we never persist raw prompt text in control plane logs.
[06:20] Tom Hayes: can you describe eviction and quotas?
[06:25] Priya Singh: eviction policy is LRU with priority tiers. we let customers set reserved capacity per tenant and a global spillover. for very latency-sensitive tenants we recommend a small reserved pool to avoid noise-induced eviction. metrics we emit: per-tenant hit_rate, eviction_count, avg_prefix_size, and warmup_latency.
[06:48] Maya Li: what about cold starts — first request after eviction — do you do async warming?
[06:53] Priya Singh: yes, warm-on-read is synchronous by default, but we support async pre-warming for known templates (scheduled via rollout hooks) so the first user sees normal latency. we can also pre-warm during canary rollout windows.
[07:10] Carlos Ruiz: how do you measure hit rate? is it by exact key match? we have many near-miss cases.
[07:17] Priya Singh: metric is exact match on hashed key. we also provide a fuzzy-match metric that groups by template hash to capture near misses due to slot differences. both are helpful.
[07:31] Alex Rivera: for your use-case, the annotated chat templates looked fairly stable per product line so we expect a conservative 60-70% effective hit rate once we do canonicalization and per-tenant reservation.
[07:45] Tom Hayes: good. any perf numbers on latency win?
[07:50] Priya Singh: big picture: cache hit bypasses the O(N^2) attention recompute for the prefix. in our internal microbench on a 4k context LlamaV2-like model, prefix hits cut generation latency by ~45-55% p95 when prefix was 8-12 tokens. end-to-end p95 went from ~360ms to ~200ms in that bench, with batching considerations.
[08:16] Maya Li: batching — how does batching interact with cached prefixes?
[08:21] Priya Singh: caching and batching are complementary. when you hit cache, you still need to batch the decoder steps; cached KV also helps because the effective compute per-token is lower. dynamic batching helps aggregate decoder steps but increases latency tail if not tuned. we recommend latency-SLO aware batching with max batch size and max wait thresholds.
[08:44] Alex Rivera: we have an internal feature called continuous batching that adapts to traffic; in practice you tune it to keep p95 within your SLOs. Priya, any numbers for tradeoff of batch size vs p95?
[08:56] Priya Singh: roughly: when you increase batch size from 1 to 8, throughput increases ~6x but p95 can increase by 20-70ms depending on queue. that's why SLO-based throttling is important. Cached prefixes reduce per-request op so they shrink the incremental p95 penalty from batching.
[09:17] Carlos Ruiz: security-wise, you said you use a keyed HMAC for cache keys. where is the key stored for on-prem?
[09:25] Priya Singh: customers can provide their KMS via our integration; the HMAC key can be seeded from customer's KMS so control plane never sees raw key material. for Private deployments we can also run HSM-backed signing locally.
[09:39] Tom Hayes: audit logs — do you log cache hits with any prompt material?
[09:45] Alex Rivera: logs are metadata only: key hash, tenant id, model id, hit/miss, latency. we don't log plaintext prompt. if you need request-level audit, that's opt-in and controlled by you within your VPC.
[09:59] Maya Li: what about multi-tenant attacks — like trying to infer another tenant's prefix by probing?
[10:06] Priya Singh: threat model recognized. mitigations: per-tenant namespaces + request rate limiting + monitoring for suspicious hit patterns. also we avoid returning any signals that could leak presence of other tenants' prefixes beyond standard API error messages.
[10:24] Tom Hayes: curious about cache warmup cost — does warming cost similar tokens as normal generation?
[10:29] Priya Singh: warm-on-read does cost the same compute as generating the prefix once. pre-warming is the same; that's why for expensive prefixes we encourage scheduled warmups during off-peak.
[10:40] Alex Rivera: Priya, you mentioned a shared bench spreadsheet — can you point them to that?
[10:44] Priya Singh: yeah, we'll share the prefix_cache_benchmarks.xlsx and a short doc outlining canonicalization rules. link: https://redwood.internal/docs/prefix_cache_benchmarks.xlsx (note: sharing via secure drive).
[10:57] Carlos Ruiz: for on-prem we need to simulate our traffic. what config do you need to run the synthetic bench?
[11:03] Priya Singh: we need: representative prompt templates, token length distribution, concurrency profile (RPS), and model/quantization choices. we'll run the bench on both Dedicate and Private-like setups to give expected hit-rates and memory needs.
[11:20] Maya Li: can you also include cost delta estimates?
[11:23] Alex Rivera: yes we'll include estimated token-cost savings and compute delta for maintaining cache memory.
[11:30] Tom Hayes: any gotchas with rollout — we have many templates and a big downstream of agents, how do we safely roll this?
[11:38] Priya Singh: rollout approach: pilot with a few high-volume templates, enable template-level cache and monitor hit_rate and warmup_latency. then expand to more templates. we usually run canaries per-tenant and have automatic fallback to no-cache for templates that regress quality or latency.
[11:55] Maya Li: what about reranking or internal evals that rely on exact logits — are cached prefixes safe there?
[12:02] Priya Singh: if you need exact floating logits we caution: quantization + kernel differences can slightly change logits. for sensitive rerank you might disable cache or pin a quantization/profile. we note this in the docs.
[12:18] Carlos Ruiz: do you have observability dashboards out-of-the-box?
[12:22] Alex Rivera: yes — per-route and per-tenant dashboards: hit_rate, miss_latency, warmup_latency, eviction_count, memory_usage. we can add custom probes if you want end-to-end traces.
[12:36] Tom Hayes: good. anything else on multi-tenant safety?
[12:40] Priya Singh: two final notes: 1) never mix tenant namespaces in a single hashed key space — always include tenant id in the composite; 2) consider tenant-level throttles and anomaly detection to protect shared pools.
[12:56] Maya Li: ok this is helpful. can you sketch an example cache key?
[13:00] Priya Singh: example (conceptual): HMAC(key, tenant:po-123|model:gpt-like-v2|tmpl:sha256(...)|plen:8|quant:int8|compile:v3) — hashed. stored metadata has canonical_template_id and version.
[13:22] Tom Hayes: do we need to rotate HMAC pepper periodically?
[13:25] Priya Singh: yes rotation is supported; we keep a key version header so older entries remain addressable until eviction. rotation schedule is a customer choice but 90 days is common.
[13:40] Alex Rivera: quick run through recommended config for Pacific Orbit's initial pilot: per-tenant soft reservation 10% of cache memory, canonicalization rules for top 50 templates, quant profile fp16 or int8 (decide based on bench), and dynamic batching knobs tuned for 300ms p95.
[14:02] Maya Li: sounds good. can you estimate memory for our projected 200 QPS with avg prefix 10 tokens?
[14:09] Priya Singh: rough calc: each KV cell ~ 2-3KB for that model in fp16; with 200 QPS and expected ~20k active unique prefixes you'd need ~40-60GB. with int8 it drops ~30%. we'll run detailed math in the bench.
[14:30] Carlos Ruiz: ok, please include hardware suggestions; our fleet is mixed.
[14:34] Alex Rivera: will do — we'll give memory and throughput guidance per GPU class (A100/H100/L4 equivalent).
[14:43] Tom Hayes: any final security/regulatory notes?
[14:46] Priya Singh: SOC2/ISO controls are in our security pack, KMS integrations for keying, and audit logs can be sent to your SIEM in VPC deployment. also we dont persist user PII in control plane.
[15:00] Alex Rivera: wrap up — we'll send the bench spreadsheet, security docs, and a proposal for the cache key and quota config. schedule on-prem bench next week if possible.
[15:12] Tom Hayes: thanks everyone. next step: Carlos will send the template exports, Alex will send pricing, Priya will run bench.
[15:20] Maya Li: thanks all.
[15:25] (call ends)

Notes: transcript contains typical auto-transcription noise; some product names abbreviated (e.g., Redwood Dedicate -> Redwood Dedicated). Shared artifacts referenced: prefix_cache_benchmarks.xlsx (secure link), canonicalization_rules.md, security_pack_SOC2.pdf.
